A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same UGM2N research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched despite appendix reorganization and renumbering.

before.justification: V1 reports original PDE simulations, mesh-adaptation comparisons, timing measurements and loss-function and iteration ablations, including Tables 1–2 and Figures 3–9.

after.justification: V2 retains those original experiments and adds training-size, boundary-treatment, sensitivity, timing and geometric-robustness results in the main text and appendices.

M1.justification: V2 adds an evaluated variant that moves boundary nodes using post-hoc clip-to-boundary projection (Appendix E.4), whereas v1 fixes boundary nodes. The default node-patch architecture, M-Uniform objective and iterative adaptation algorithm remain unchanged.

E1.justification: V2 substantially expands evaluation to non-convex meshes, irregular meshes with varying node degrees, anisotropic meshes, and random polygonal domains with Gaussian-mixture solutions (Appendices E.2, E.7–E.8). It also mentions a Tohoku tsunami case, although its supplementary results are outside the supplied PDFs.

E2.justification: The principal comparator set remains MA, M2N and UM2N. For the existing moving-cylinder and supersonic-wedge qualitative cases, v1 Figure 8 shows UGM2N alone; v2 Appendix E.9 adds M2N and UM2N comparisons in Figure 19 and reports MA failures.

E3.justification: V2 introduces controlled evaluations over five loss scales, training sets of 4/8/16 flow fields, and fixed versus projected boundary-node movement. New robustness protocols specify 100 small non-convex meshes, 10 irregular meshes and 1,000 random polygons, with additional absolute-error and positive-ER-fraction reporting. The original training split and headline PDE settings are retained.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's loss-function and iteration ablations, v2 adds loss-scale sensitivity, training-volume and boundary-treatment studies, displacement-based convergence diagnostics, and component-level timing analysis. It also directly tests robustness when mesh regularity assumptions fail and across randomized geometries.

E5.justification: V1 reports ten-trial average timing without uncertainty estimates. V2 introduces five runs per loss-scale value, variability bars in Figure 10, and mean±standard-deviation reporting for tangling, timing and random-domain ER (Tables 5, 8 and 11). The right-hand Figure 10 bars describe variability across loss scales; the ten timing repetitions do not represent an increased run count.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 and the original equidistribution scores remain unchanged, but v2 adds substantial new results. Table 11 reports UGM2N ER of 13.99%±21.05% and a positive-ER fraction of 0.807, versus 0.110 for MA and 0.245 for UM2N. Other additions quantify boundary projection, training-size effects, timing and irregular/anisotropic performance; these are additional experimental results rather than revised headline scores.

T1.justification: V2 Appendix A adds an explicit Monge–Ampère determinant equation and defines its convex potential and coordinate mapping. The existing total-variance derivation and mesh-regularity approximation are retained in Appendix B.2. Its added convergence discussion and displacement measurements do not supply a new convergence proof.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution statements and conclusion retain the same claims about unsupervised node-patch adaptation, M-Uniform loss, generalization, efficiency and error reduction without tangling. The expanded experiments principally support those existing claims.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive interpretations of boundary projection, training-data scaling and convergence, and identifies CPU–GPU transfers as a practical timing bottleneck. Its limitations discussion incorporates the irregular-mesh findings, qualifies applicability to more extreme meshes and newly acknowledges rotation dependence (Appendix F).

D1.justification: V2 explicitly clarifies that training does not dynamically update mesh nodes, documents generation procedures for added mesh tests and explains boundary projection and CPU-based interpolation transfers. It also specifies 24 GB GPU memory and practical capacity. The original architecture, optimizer, split and training-time disclosures remain unchanged.

R1.justification: V2 adds the Graph Attention Networks citation and explicitly credits Rowbottom et al. with proving avoidance of mesh entanglement. Their G-Adaptive/G-Adaptivity reference is updated to its conference publication, rather than introducing a separate work. The broader research positioning remains intact.

P1.justification: Most existing scientific prose and the main section sequence are retained. V2 makes localized wording corrections and explanatory additions, updates affiliations and acknowledgments, and consolidates previously separate results and metrics appendices under Appendix E.

P2.justification: V2 adds seven figures and seven tables displaying the new analyses. It also relocates retained displays, compacts the author block, redraws Figure 9's labels and legend, and removes the text–caption overlap around Figure 2 visible in v1. Most original figure content is retained.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the evidence for generalization by testing irregular and anisotropic meshes that v1 identified as insufficiently validated, alongside 1,000 randomized domains. Controlled ablations, variability reporting and timing breakdowns make robustness and practical limits much easier to assess. The unchanged abstract's guaranteed-error-reduction claim conflicts with newly reported failures, and convergence remains unproved, but the added validation and transparency provide a substantial net improvement.
